concept: Game product safety labeling and workshop hazards
summary: Source-anchored research for Game product safety labeling and workshop hazards. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: OSHA says engineering and work-practice controls should be the primary feasible means of reducing toxic chemical exposure; NIOSH describes source-capture ventilation for volatile printing-press emissions. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC’s small-parts ban covers products intended for children under three, but exempts books and other articles made of paper; entirely paper pieces detached during use-and-abuse testing are also excluded from the small-part test. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC permits reliance on component-supplier lead-test evidence only with due care and access to underlying test documentation, including valid testing by a CPSC-accepted laboratory. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Reliance on a component supplier’s lead test or certificate requires due care and access to underlying test documentation; a bare supplier assurance is insufficient under CPSC’s explanation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

OSHA’s printing-press roll-cleaning case rejects the minor-servicing exception when workers bypass guards and lack effective alternative protection, even when cleaning is routine, repetitive and integral to production. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Small-parts warning requirements depend on the product and intended age, including applicable products for ages 3–6; advertising for toys subject to the warning must carry it too. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC says paper and ordinary CMYK process printing inks can avoid third-party lead testing under material determinations; this does not remove the lead-content limit or the obligation to certify compliance. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The CMYK lead determination excludes spot colors, non-CMYK inks, inks outside the substrate and specified after-treatment printing; it cannot be extended automatically to every printed finish. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-04)

CPSC identifies specific choking-warning labeling rules for products containing small parts and intended for children between three and six; that scope should be checked separately from paper exemptions to the under-three small-parts ban. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
CPSC says accessible children’s-product components must meet a total lead limit of 100 ppm and paint or similar surface coatings a separate 90 ppm limit. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

OSHA requires guarding where operation exposes employees to injury and lists guillotine cutters; the guard must prevent access to the danger zone during the operating cycle, rather than merely warn. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

UK HSE identifies failure to refit guards as a major cause of printing-industry accidents. This supports guard-restoration checks as an operational concern, rather than establishing a US legal requirement. (low confidence)

OSHA lists guillotine cutters among machines usually requiring point-of-operation guarding; hand tools for placing or removing material supplement rather than replace required guards. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC classifies a children’s product by primary intended use for children aged 12 or younger, considering reasonable manufacturer statements, marketing, consumer recognition and age-determination guidance; an age label alone does not control classification. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC treats traditional playing cards and similar games appealing to a general audience as general-use products; child-oriented features or junior packaging can change that classification. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

For toys primarily intended for children aged 12 or younger, CPSC requires applicable third-party testing by an accepted laboratory and a Children’s Product Certificate; the manufacturer or importer must identify applicable toy-standard sections. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC distinguishes ASTM F963’s under-14 toy scope from the federal third-party-testing threshold for products intended primarily for children 12 or younger. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC exempts labeling, instructions and producer markings from third-party laboratory testing, while requiring CPC certification of all applicable toy-standard sections. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Children’s products need permanent tracking information on product and packaging to the extent practicable, including the responsible firm, production date and location, and identifying production information such as a batch or run number. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC distinguishes a toy’s substantive flammability obligations from premarket testing: the FHSA prohibits hazardous flammable children’s toys even though this requirement does not mandate premarket or third-party testing. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

OSHA’s printing interpretation limits the minor-servicing exception to routine, repetitive, integral production work with effective alternative protection. Normal guillotine blade changing requires an energy-control procedure with lockout/tagout and any necessary guarding. (low confidence) (verified as of 2004-04-07)
The MBM-hosted manual describes a movable guard and two-hand control as cutting safeguards for IDEAL 6655. (low confidence)

Where OSHA’s Hazard Communication standard applies, employers need a written program for chemical labels, SDSs and training; SDSs must be immediately accessible, and training covers initial assignment and new chemical hazards. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

NIOSH identifies inhalation and skin-contact hazards during press cleaning. Its printing LEV example reports vapor and dust measurement reductions of 83 percent and 67 percent; these are case results, not workshop performance predictions. (low confidence)

A NIOSH educational vignette links visual symptoms to an amine-containing additive used with water-based ink. NIOSH calls the story loosely based on evaluations and cautions that its facility-specific recommendations may not generalize. (low confidence)

OSHA’s lithography guidance identifies repeated reaching, pinching, prolonged standing and low-table bending in hand collation; it recommends reachable stacks, adjusted work height, posture variation and reduced exposure time. (low confidence)

CPSC’s labeling overview still names ASTM F963-17, whereas its Toy Safety FAQ names ASTM F963-23 with an April 20, 2024 effective date. This is a mismatch between the two cited pages, not evidence that both editions currently govern. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

CPSC allows a reusable storage container to satisfy on-product marking for some multi-piece children’s products; it also says there is no tracking-label exemption based on business size. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

NIOSH identifies press-cleaning solvent vapors and skin absorption as printing hazards; its control guidance describes local exhaust that captures vapor near the press and exhausts it outside with replacement air. (low confidence)

In the printing study summarized by NIOSH, local exhaust reduced measured real-time vapor by 83 percent and dust by 67 percent; these are study results, not a guaranteed reduction for another workshop. (low confidence)
For employers using hazardous workplace chemicals, OSHA requires labels, safety data sheets and worker training about hazards and protective measures. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

OSHA’s lithography guidance identifies repetitive forceful paper gripping, awkward wrist postures and bending in finishing work; suggested controls include smaller handled stacks, neutral hand postures and adjustable work surfaces. (low confidence)
